title: Association Between Quantitative Brushing Efficacy and Dental Caries Severity in Schoolchildren
content: Background: Although toothbrushing is widely recognized as a cornerstone of caries prevention, oral hygiene has traditionally been assessed using self-reported frequency or categorical plaque indices. Evidence regarding the relationship between objectively quantified brushing efficacy and cumulative caries severity remains limited. This study evaluated the association between a quantitative brushing efficacy index and dental caries severity among schoolchildren. Methods: A cross-sectional analytical study was conducted among 200 schoolchildren examined during a community dental campaign in 2025. Caries was assessed using Decayed, Missing, Filled Teeth indices following Word Health Organization criteria. Severe caries was defined as Decayed, Missing, Filled Teeth ≥5. Oral hygiene was measured using a brushing efficacy index, expressed as the percentage of biofilm removed after supervised brushing. Associations were evaluated using chi-square tests and logistic regression models adjusted for age and sex. Results: Caries prevalence was 95.5%, with a mean Decayed, Missing, Filled Teeth of 4.99 ± 2.96. Severe caries was observed in 49% of participants. No statistically significant differences were found across tertiles of brushing efficacy (χ² (2) =2.18; p=0.336). In regression analysis, each 10% increase in brushing efficacy was not significantly associated with severe caries (adjusted OR=0.92; 95% CI: 0.81–1.03; p=0.154), although a protective trend was observed. Conclusions: This population exhibited an extremely high burden of dental caries. Quantitative brushing efficacy showed a non-significant protective trend, suggesting that in high-risk contexts, caries severity is influenced by multifactorial determinants beyond isolated oral hygiene performance.
